Dear Ms. Okafor,

I am writing to apply for the Junior Data Analyst position at Ridgeway Freight Solutions, which I found on your careers page. I graduated in May with a B.S. in Statistics from Lakeview State University, and I have spent the last year building the kind of analysis work this role describes.

During my senior capstone, I worked with a team of four to forecast weekly shipment volumes for a regional grocery distributor. I cleaned about 180,000 rows of dispatch records in Python, built a set of SQL views to join them with carrier data, and presented a dashboard in Power BI that the operations group still uses. Our model cut forecast error by roughly 14 percent compared with their old spreadsheet.

Your posting mentions SQL, Tableau, and working closely with operations teams. I have used all three, and I enjoy translating messy questions from non-technical colleagues into something they can act on. My resume is attached, along with a short sample analysis of public port-delay data.

Thank you for considering my application. I would welcome the chance to talk about how I could contribute to your team.

Best regards,
Eli Brandt

Dear Mr. Lindqvist,

Thank you for taking the time to speak with me today about the Junior Data Analyst role on your customer analytics team. I really enjoyed our conversation, especially the discussion about how the team decides which delivery metrics to track when they conflict with each other.

The exercise you gave me, looking at the late-delivery data for the Midwest region, was a good test. I was careful about the duplicate scan records you mentioned, and I think my explanation of the seasonal dip in March made sense, but I would like to go back over the regression assumptions with you if there is time.

I am still very interested in the role and in working with a team that takes the operations side seriously. Please let me know if you need anything else from me, such as a writing sample or a copy of my analysis notebook.

Thank you again for your time.

Kind regards,
Priya Raman

Dear Mr. Haddad,

I hope you are doing well. I am applying for junior data analyst jobs this month, and I wanted to ask whether you would be willing to act as a reference for me. You supervised me for almost two years at Greenmoor Medical Supply, and I think you know my work better than anyone else I am considering.

If you agree, the companies would most likely call you or send a short questionnaire about my analytical work, my reliability, and how I handled the inventory reporting project. I can send you my updated resume and a list of the three or four points I would like you to speak to, so you do not have to prepare from scratch.

I understand if you are too busy right now. If it would be easier, I am happy to talk on the phone for ten minutes.

Thank you for considering this. I appreciate everything you taught me about working with messy data under pressure.

Best,
Tomasz Wierzbicki

I want to work at Ridgeway Freight Solutions because freight is one of the few industries where a small improvement in a data process shows up immediately in cost, delivery time, and driver schedules. Your team's public write-up about reducing empty backhauls in the Southeast network was the first thing that made me want to apply. I read it twice and wrote down the three questions I still had about the method.

I am also drawn to the fact that your analytics group sits next to dispatch and warehouse operations rather than in a separate building. In my capstone, the hardest part was not the modeling. It was figuring out what the dispatchers actually needed to see before their morning meeting. I want a job where that kind of feedback loop is normal.

I have a background in statistics and SQL, and I have worked with logistics data before, though at a smaller scale. I would like to learn how your teams handle carrier data that arrives late or in inconsistent formats, and I would like to bring the same care I put into my own cleaning scripts to your reporting work.

I was put in charge of the statistics tutoring lab's data in my second year. The sign-in records were in three different spreadsheets, each maintained by a different staff member, and about a fifth of the student IDs did not match across them. The department wanted a report on which courses were getting the most visits before the budget meeting, and I had two weeks to produce it.

My first instinct was to start building the report anyway and fix the mismatches as I went. After a few hours I realized that every chart I made was quietly wrong, because some students were being counted twice and others were missing entirely. I stopped and spent most of a week on the matching problem instead.

I wrote a short Python script that normalized the IDs, flagged the ones it could not match, and sent those back to the staff members who had entered them. Many were typos. I did not know the answer to all of them, so I kept a log of every decision and why I made it.

The report was about three days late, but the budget committee trusted the numbers, and the coordinator told me later that the log was the reason.

What I learned is that the slow, unglamorous part of the work usually decides whether the results mean anything. Now I check whether the data can answer the question before I build anything, and I write down what I changed.

The project I am proudest of is a small dashboard I built for my university's housing office last spring. The office was tracking maintenance requests in a shared spreadsheet, and the director wanted to know which buildings were slowest to get repairs done. Nobody had ever calculated that, so there was no baseline to compare against.

I pulled eighteen months of request records, cleaned the timestamps, and calculated the time from submission to completion for each building. The first version showed one building as far worse than the rest, but when I checked the notes I found that the office had been closing tickets as soon as a contractor was scheduled, not after the work was finished. I rebuilt the metric with the completion date from the contractor's invoices and reran everything.

The final dashboard had three views: average wait by building, a monthly trend, and a list of open requests older than thirty days. The director now uses it at the start of every staff meeting. Two buildings were moved to a different contractor based on what it showed.

I am proud of it because the technical part was not hard. What mattered was catching the definition problem before anyone made decisions from the wrong number.

Thanks for reading this. Happy to chat whenever works.

Eli Brandt
